title: Strangers in the rule
hookLine: a small practice of welcome: Abraham ran from his tent door to meet three strangers, and the rabbis called welcoming guests greater than receiving God's presence
tomorrow: why would giving the money away be called the true bargain?

cards: It's possible to know a delivery driver's car better than a neighbor's name. Abraham is sitting in the door of his tent, in the plains of Mamre, "in the heat of the day." The hour when nobody moves.
The Torah says the LORD appeared to him there. And then: "he lift up his eyes and looked, and, lo, three men stood by him: and when he saw them, he ran to meet them from the tent door."

teach.h: A MORSEL, AND THEN A FEAST.
teach.b: An old man, running, in the heat, toward people he doesn't know. He bows. He begs them to stay: let a little water be fetched to wash your feet, rest under the tree, I'll bring a morsel of bread.
Then he hurries to Sarah to bake cakes, runs to the herd for a calf, and stands by them under the tree while they eat. A morsel, he said. He brought a feast.
The strangers turn out to be messengers, carrying the news that Sarah will have a son.
Christians hear this scene in a New Testament line: "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares." The rabbis drew a Jewish teaching from it.
The LORD had appeared to Abraham, and Abraham left that moment to run to the guests.
So the Talmud says it outright: welcoming guests is greater than receiving the Divine Presence.
Jews call it hachnasat orchim, bringing in guests.
A stranger in the rule doesn't need a feast. It starts with the running: noticing first, moving first, offering the morsel.

how: Jews call welcoming guests hachnasat orchim and trace it to Abraham at Mamre. Christians read the same scene with Hebrews 13:2. Some people write one small act of welcome for strangers into their rule.

games.q: what does “strangers in the rule” mean?
o: a polite rule to keep strangers at a safe distance
a list of guests invited to a holiday dinner each year
a small practice of welcome toward people you don't know

games.q: Abraham at Mamre: tap the pairs.
p: when Abraham sat in his tent door
what he promised; a feast is what came
what strangers may turn out to be

s: Abraham waited for the strangers to ask before offering them anything
he saw them and ran to meet them from the tent door.
the Talmud says welcoming guests is greater than receiving the Divine Presence
the rabbis learned it from Abraham leaving the LORD's appearance to run to the guests.
Abraham served the three men exactly the small morsel he promised
he promised a morsel, then brought cakes, a calf, and stood by them while they ate.

games.q: a family has just moved in down the street. by Abraham at Mamre, what fits?
o: knock first, with something small, before they have to ask.
wait for them to come and introduce themselves when ready.
give them a few months to settle before saying anything.
games.why: Abraham didn't wait at the tent. He saw the strangers, ran to meet them, and offered a morsel first.

practice: Sit facing a door, if you can, the way Abraham sat in his tent door. Let your hands rest open on your knees. Bring to mind one person you pass but have never welcomed, and choose the first small thing you'd offer.

wordCard.voice: Strangers in the rule: a small practice of welcome, written into your rule, moving first toward people you don't know, the way Abraham ran from his tent door.

orig.note: Hebrew, Jewish teaching: 'bringing in guests', the duty of hospitality traced to Abraham.

carryVoice: Take this with you: the stranger. He promised a morsel and ran to bring a feast. Day 1660, and the door's open.
